name: MACS lift

card.summary: A short-scar facelift that hangs the lower and mid face from above with purse-string sutures along a purely vertical vector; surgeon series report quicker recovery.
card.note: Evidence is mostly from the surgeons who developed and promote it; limits are discussed for the lower face and neck.

quick.overview:
The MACS (minimal access cranial suspension) lift is a short-scar facelift that uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue upward with permanent purse-string sutures anchored to firm tissue above. It was proposed in 2002 as a modification of the S-lift.

Its developers report operating times of about 2 to 2.5 hours under local anesthesia and a quicker recovery than classic facelifts, with results they describe as comparably stable. Independent reviews have discussed advantages and limitations.
quick.mechanism: Purse-string sutures lift the neck and lower face along a vertical vector with no lateral tension; an optional third, malar suture adds midface correction in the extended version.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says less skin is raised, so bleeding and nerve-injury risk are lower than with traditional facelifts, but general facelift risks still apply, including hematoma, scarring and nerve injury. Reviews have outlined limitations for the lower third of the face.

lead: The minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift is a short-scar facelift that tightens a sagging jawline, jowls, neck and cheeks by lifting them upward and fixing them in place, so the lower and middle face look firmer and more defined. It uses a vertical vector, involves no lateral tension, and in its authors' description can be performed under local anesthesia in 2 to 2.5 hours.[1] It was proposed in 2002 as a modified version of the S-lift, suspending tissue with permanent purse-string sutures.[2]

People who want a visibly lifted lower face with a shorter scar and a shorter recovery than a classic facelift are the typical candidates. Wikipedia states that the MACS lift uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue vertically from above, raises less skin so bleeding and nerve injury risk is lower, takes about 2.5 hours against 3.5 for a traditional facelift, and has a recovery of 2 to 3 weeks versus 3 to 4.[3] The developers write that it reduces recovery time and morbidity and that results are as stable as more classic, extended techniques.[1]

It exists in a simple version with two purse-string sutures for the neck and lower face and an extended version that adds a third, malar suture for the midface.[4] A 2022 systematic review described it as one of the most popular short-scar facelift techniques and credited its development to Tonnard and Vaerpele.[12] The literature is dominated by surgeons who use the technique; independent assessments exist, including a 2026 meta-analysis against the deep SMAS lift and a review of its advantages and limitations.[13][5]

chain: Short incision in front of the ear
Purse-string sutures lift the neck, jowls and cheeks vertically
Firmer jawline and fuller midface with a short, hidden scar
angle.text: The procedure repositions sagging facial tissue upward and anchors it to firm tissue at the temple, which restores a tighter jawline and neck contour. Patients choose it when they want a lift with a shorter scar and a shorter recovery period than a classic facelift.

infobox: Local possible; 2 to 2.5 hours per authors[1]

paras: The technique uses permanent purse-string sutures placed through a short temporal-preauricular incision and anchored to deep temporal fascia, lifting the tissues vertically.[2][4] Skin undermining is limited, and the sutures loop through the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the platysma before being anchored above.[14] In the developers' 2005 report of 450 cases performed between November 1999 and February 2005, the neck was corrected with extended submental liposuction and strong vertical traction on the lateral platysma by a first purse-string suture.[6] Surgeons have proposed ways to optimise results[6] and a deep-plane hybrid, the minimal access deep plane extended (MADE) vertical facelift, that combines features of deep-plane and short-incision lifts.[7]

A third, malar suture in the extended version is described by its authors as giving volumetric restoration of the midface, a softer nasolabial fold and better support of the lower eyelid.[4] A 2020 report described an elastic-thread modification of the MACS lift for the lower and middle third of the face.[18]

Facelift methods range from traditional rhytidectomy and deep-plane or composite techniques to limited-incision approaches such as lateral SMASectomy, the S-lift and the MACS lift, and suspension-suture lifts such as APTOS and Contour Threads.[16] A 2007 review noted that most of the literature consists of surgeons describing their own methods and results, with few comparative studies.[16]

Wikipedia traces facelift history from Eugen Holländer's first reported operation in Berlin in 1901 through Tord Skoog's subfacial dissection in the late 1960s and 1970s and the 1976 description of the SMAS by Mitz and Peyronie, with a later period focused on smaller scars, volume restoration and cranial lifting.[3] The MACS lift belongs to that last group.

A 2025 narrative review of facelift techniques and the retaining ligaments of the face grouped the MACS lift with the ligament-preserving techniques, in contrast to deep-plane and extended SMAS facelifts, which release ligaments and allow greater mobilization of midfacial and neck tissue.[15] The platysma-SMAS plication facelift, published in 2010, was presented as an evolution intended to balance invasiveness and recovery time, with the authors noting that the MACS lift has limitations in its vectors and in its effect on the neck.[17]

A 2008 article examined indications and limitations of the MACS lift for the lower third of the face.[8] A later review discussed its advantages and limitations for facial rejuvenation.[5] A 2019 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery described it as a minimally invasive face and neck lift that, in a properly selected patient, is an effective technique with high physician and patient satisfaction.[14] The technique has also been used to treat complications of APTOS thread lifting, together with fat grafting.[9]

Wikipedia's discussion of short-scar facelifts says they suit people with deep nasolabial folds and sagging structures who still have a firm, well-contoured neck, and describes them as less invasive with less downtime.[3]

Wikipedia gives a MACS recovery of about 2 to 3 weeks against 3 to 4 weeks for a traditional facelift, with the scar placed in front of the ear instead of behind it.[3] The developers report that local anesthesia is possible and that operating time is about 2 to 2.5 hours.[1]

Facelift costs vary widely by country and surgeon; Wikipedia cites 2008 ranges from about US$2,500 in India and Panama to US$15,000 in the US and Canada, and 2009 figures of mostly 4,000 to 9,000 pounds in Europe.[3]

As with other facelifts, risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and anesthesia reactions; Wikipedia states that short-incision methods carry lower bleeding and nerve-injury risk because less skin is raised.[3] Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common facelift complication, the greater auricular nerve as the most commonly injured sensory nerve, and smoking as a factor that raises skin-necrosis risk; it also notes possible hair loss at incisions in hair-bearing scalp and changes in ear position.[3]
In the 2022 systematic review, no major complications were reported across the included studies, and four of six studies reported minor complications.[12]

Studies are mostly surgeon-reported series. The 2007 paper describes the procedure and reports stability comparable to extended techniques in the authors' view.[1] The 2005 series covered 450 operations by the developers.[6]

A 2022 systematic review searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central and Google Scholar and included six studies with 739 patients treated with the MACS lift. All six reported relatively high satisfaction, no major complications were reported, and three studies reported a shorter procedure than a conventional facelift.[12]

A 2026 meta-analysis compared the deep SMAS lift with the MACS lift: of 20 studies covering 7,716 patients, four met inclusion criteria, covering 286 patients (186 MACS, 100 SMAS). Aesthetic outcomes and complications were comparable, and the MACS lift had a significantly shorter surgical duration (SMD 2.05, 95% CI 1.61 to 2.48). The authors called for further research to establish efficacy and safety profiles.[13]

A 2014 retrospective analysis compared platelet-rich plasma with fat grafting, with and without MACS lift, on recovery time and aesthetic outcome.[10] A 2018 study examined how facelift practice evolved with new techniques,[11] and a 2024 review used American Board of Plastic Surgery tracer data to examine clinical practice patterns in facelift surgery over 15 years.[19] No randomized comparisons with other facelifts were found.

timeline.event: S-lift described; later basis for MACS. The developers' series of 450 cases began in November 1999.[2][6]
